planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in moist to wet, humus-rich soil at a meadow low spot, pond edge, or streambank; this high-elevation native tolerates cold winters but needs consistent spring moisture through bloom.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Rocky Mountain iris is the widespread native blue flag of western North America, found from North Dakota and British Columbia south to California and New Mexico in mountain meadows, streambanks, and marshy ground up to 9,000 feet elevation. It sends up pale to deep violet-blue flowers with darker veining in late spring above narrow, grayish-green foliage, and forms slowly spreading colonies from creeping rhizomes. In the garden it thrives at a pond margin, in a wet meadow planting, or in any low spot that stays consistently moist through spring, though it tolerates a drier dormancy once summer arrives. Divide congested clumps every several years in fall to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade; beachhead iris is extremely cold-hardy and needs no winter protection even in far-northern gardens.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions shallowly in fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; beachhead iris is a circumpolar native reaching its southern limit in Alaska, coastal British Columbia, and Maine, where it grows in wet meadows, tundra seeps, and beach margins. Its distinctive flowers have standards reduced to small bristles, leaving the broad, heart-shaped falls in deep blue-violet to purple-blue (occasionally pale lavender) to do the visual work. Extremely cold-hardy, it shrugs off harsh northern winters and is a good choice for rain gardens, pond margins, and boggy ground in cool-summer climates. Divide crowded clumps in fall every few years to keep plants vigorous and free-flowering.

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil; established clumps resent disturbance so divide only when needed.

directions: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall as rains return, setting fans shallowly in fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Oregon iris is native to open prairies, logged clearings, and oak and conifer forest openings of southwestern Washington and northwestern Oregon, forming low, slowly spreading clumps of narrow, semi-evergreen foliage topped by lavender-blue to purple flowers in late spring, with white, cream, pink, or yellow forms occurring in the wild. Once established it is genuinely drought tolerant through summer but will not tolerate soggy feet or heavy clay, so plant in a well-drained meadow, rock garden, or pollinator border. Note that the rhizomes and foliage are toxic if ingested and can cause skin irritation, so handle with care.
sources: East Multnomah Soil and Water Conservation District

planting.note: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall into well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in light shade to sun; give it little supplemental water once established, mimicking its dry-summer native climate.

directions: Divide and transplant rhizome clumps in fall into well-drained, neutral to slightly acidic soil in light partial shade to sun. Del Norte County iris is native to open, mixed-evergreen woodland and sunny meadow edges of southwestern Oregon and the Klamath Ranges of northern California, forming dense, evergreen tufts of narrow foliage low to the ground. Its short flower stems carry one or two blooms in a striking range of colors from golden yellow and apricot to cream, pink, and purple, opening in spring. It is one of the parent species behind the popular Pacific Coast Hybrid irises and prefers the same cool, wet-winter, dry-summer regime, needing little water once established but appreciating excellent drainage. Use it in a woodland edge, rock garden, or dry shade border in mild-winter Pacific climates.
sources: Theodore Payne Foundation Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil at a bog edge or wet meadow; grows in full sun where soil stays wet, or partial shade if the site dries somewhat between rains.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in full sun where the ground stays reliably wet, or partial shade if conditions are drier; slender blue flag is a delicate-looking but tough native of Atlantic coastal plain wetlands from Maine to Georgia, with a scattered inland presence in the southern Appalachians. Wiry, grass-like foliage and slim flower stems distinguish it from the bulkier blue flag iris (I. versicolor), and its seed capsules are sharply three-angled (prismatic) rather than rounded, the source of its common name cubeseed iris. It tolerates periods of standing fresh or brackish water, making it a good fit for a rain garden, bog planting, or pond margin. Divide crowded clumps every few years in fall to maintain bloom.

common_name: Clara Goula Louisiana Iris (Ruffled White DeBaillon Medal Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Clara Goula is one of the most celebrated Louisiana iris cultivars, bred by Charles Arny Jr. and registered in 1975.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Clara Goula, hybridized by Charles Arny Jr. and registered in 1975, bears tall, elegantly ruffled white to pale cream self flowers with a small yellow signal on a well-branched, statuesque plant blooming early to midseason. It went on to win both the American Iris Society's DeBaillon Award (1982) and the DeBaillon Medal (1987), the highest honor given to a Louisiana iris, and remains a benchmark white cultivar and popular parent in later breeding. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet soil, making it an excellent choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Praline Festival Louisiana Iris (Cream and Rose-Tan Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Praline Festival, from the cross 'Valera' x 'President Hedley', was hybridized by Dorman Haymon and registered in 1992.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Praline Festival, hybridized by Dorman Haymon from the cross 'Valera' x 'President Hedley' and registered in 1992, carries ruffled cream flowers heavily veined and dusted in rose-tan with a yellow-gold signal streaked green down the full length of the falls, the rose-tan style arms edged in cream — a color combination reminiscent of its Louisiana namesake confection. It blooms in midseason on a well-branched stalk. Like other Louisiana iris it grows best in consistently damp to wet, fertile soil, making it well suited to a pond margin, rain garden, or low, naturally moist spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Acadian Miss Louisiana Iris (Ruffled White DeBaillon Medal Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Acadian Miss, from the cross 'Clyde Redmond' x 'Clara Goula', was hybridized by Charles Arny Jr. and registered in 1980.

directions: Plant rhizomes in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Acadian Miss, hybridized by Charles Arny Jr. from the cross 'Clyde Redmond' x 'Clara Goula' and registered in 1980, bears ruffled white flowers with a yellow-green signal and green style arms on a well-branched, early-to-midseason stalk. It went on to earn the American Iris Society's DeBaillon Medal in 1990, the society's highest honor for a Louisiana iris. Like other Louisiana iris it thrives in consistently damp to wet, fertile soil, making it a strong choice for a pond edge, rain garden, or naturally low, poorly drained spot in the landscape. Divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer or early fall to maintain vigor.
